title: Best Budget Android Phones with Good Camera: Top Picks Compared
text:
For most buyers who want the strongest camera without stepping into flagship territory, a Google Pixel “a” series phone is the safest pick; the Samsung Galaxy A-series suits people who want a bright screen and long software support, and the Nothing Phone (3a) suits anyone who wants a dedicated zoom lens at a mid-range level. Below is how these phones compare on the camera points that matter, what the makers state, and where each one gives something up.

...

## What “good camera” means on a budget phone

Megapixel counts rarely decide photo quality at this level. Reviewers usually point to three things instead: how well the processing handles difficult light, how consistent the colour is from shot to shot, and how many useful lenses the phone carries. A budget phone with a single excellent main camera and clever software will often beat a phone with four mediocre lenses. Keep that in mind when you read spec sheets.

- Main sensor and processing: This does most of the work. Most budget phones now use a roughly 50-megapixel main sensor, and the software tuning separates the good from the average.
- Ultrawide lens: Useful for rooms, buildings and group shots. Quality drops compared with the main camera on nearly every phone in this class.
- Telephoto lens: Rare under the flagship tier. A true optical zoom lens gives cleaner portraits than cropping into the main sensor.
- Night shooting: Check whether the phone has a dedicated night mode and optical image stabilisation on the main lens, both of which help in dim light.
- Video: Stabilisation and steady autofocus matter more than a high resolution label.
- Software support: Longer update promises keep camera apps and security patches current for more years.

## At a glance

| Phone | Best for | Key stated camera specs (maker) | Main limits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Google Pixel 9a | Point-and-shoot photo quality, long updates | Main camera plus ultrawide, with Google’s computational photography features; the maker states a long update commitment | No telephoto lens; charging is not the fastest in class |
| Samsung Galaxy A56 | Everyday all-rounder, bright display, long support | Roughly 50-megapixel main, ultrawide and a small macro lens, according to the maker | Macro lens is of limited use; processing is more saturated than natural |
| Nothing Phone (3a) | Zoom shots and portraits on a mid-range budget | Main camera, a telephoto lens with optical zoom and an ultrawide, per the maker | Software support window is shorter than Google or Samsung’s |
| Samsung Galaxy A36 | Lower budget with a familiar Samsung camera app | Roughly 50-megapixel main with ultrawide and macro, as listed by the maker | Weaker low-light results than the A56 class |
| Previous-generation Pixel 8a | Cheapest route to Google’s camera tuning | Main plus ultrawide, per Google’s earlier listing | Older chip; shorter remaining update period |

...

## Google Pixel 9a: the processing-first choice

Google’s strategy has long been to pair a good but not extravagant sensor with heavy computational photography. Reviewers consistently describe Pixel “a” phones as producing natural skin tones, strong dynamic range and reliable results in scenes that confuse other phones. Features such as night shooting, portrait blur, and photo editing tools that remove distractions or adjust lighting after the shot are part of Google’s software package, and the maker highlights them on its product page.

The trade-off is hardware. There is no dedicated telephoto lens, so zoomed shots rely on cropping and software upscaling. Reviewers also note that the body and the screen are less showy than rival phones. If you shoot mostly people, pets, food and street scenes in everyday light, the Pixel is the easiest recommendation in this class. If you often zoom in on distant subjects, look at the Nothing instead.

## Samsung Galaxy A56 and A36: the well-rounded options

Samsung’s A-series gives you a large, bright display, a polished camera app and a long list of shooting modes. The maker lists a roughly 50-megapixel main camera on both phones, with an ultrawide lens and a macro lens. Reviewers generally say Samsung’s colour tuning is punchier than Google’s, which looks flattering straight out of the camera, though some buyers prefer a more neutral look.

Samsung also states a long software support period for the A-series, which is a real selling point if you plan to keep the phone for years. The A56 is the better camera phone of the pair, and the A36 is the choice if you need to save money. The macro lens on both is a low-resolution add-on, and most reviewers treat it as a minor feature rather than a reason to buy.

## Nothing Phone (3a): the zoom pick

The Phone (3a) is the standout when you want optical zoom without moving up in price tier. The maker lists a main camera, an ultrawide and a telephoto lens with a modest optical zoom factor. Reviewers say the telephoto lens produces cleaner portraits and distant shots than cropping from a single sensor, although image processing is less refined than Google’s in dim conditions.

Also consider the design and software.

...

| Entry budget | A decent 50-megapixel main camera, basic night mode | Weak ultrawide, no stabilised video, slower focus |
| Upper budget | Optical stabilisation on the main lens, better processing, ultrawide | No telephoto, mid-grade video |
| Lower mid-range | Telephoto lens or the best processing, longer updates | Slower charging or fewer extras |

| Long updates plus a bright display and flexible camera app | Samsung Galaxy A56 |
| Optical zoom for portraits and distant subjects | Nothing Phone (3a) |
| The lowest outlay with a known brand | Samsung Galaxy A36 or previous-generation Pixel 8a |

title: Which Android phone should you buy in 2026?
text: Despite all the hype around flagships, you don't need to spend a fortune on your new phone. So, my pick for the best Android phone for everyone and the most reasonable choice has been unchanged in the last few months, and it's the Samsung Galaxy S25 FE. Samsung's fan edition phone is now usually sold at a big discount, so you can get a 256 gigabyte model for less than $600. The big advantage of the FE is its big 6.7-in screen, which is a huge advantage over phones like the Pixel 10a. And best of all, the S25 FE comes with a whopping 7 years of software updates, so you know you're covered for the long haul. I also really like the slim design of this phone. And it's also much lighter than flagships at just 190 g. And the battery size is still a respectable 4,900 mA hours, and you also [music] get 45-W fast charging and wireless charging as well. Honestly, I don't see any flaws at all. This phone is seriously underrated. However, if you really want the best camera at a lower price, I say go for the Pixel 10a or Pixel 9a. But again, choose the 256 GB option. The Pixel 10a is a smaller phone with a 6.3-in screen, but it has an outstanding battery that will last most users 2 days on a single charge, and it has the best camera quality at a normal price. I also really like the fun color options, and the camera system is completely flush with the back of the phone on the 10a. This phone also gets 7 years of software updates, but its biggest advantage is something that few people talk about. Those updates arrive immediately after they're released. And some of you may wonder why the Pixel 10a and not the Pixel 10. If you really want the zoom camera, only then go for the Pixel 10. But otherwise, I'd save up.

title: Mid-Range Phone Camera Test: Pixel 9a vs iPhone 16e vs A56
text:
Mid-range phones now shoot photos that embarrass cameras from three years ago. The Pixel 9a, iPhone 16e, and Galaxy A56 are the three most tested budget contenders of 2025, and each wins a different kind of shot. If you care about low light and macro, the Pixel 9a leads. If you want the cleanest single-lens detail and reliable zoom, the iPhone 16e holds up. If you want the most flexible system with an ultrawide and better color punch, the Galaxy A56 is the safer pick. Below is a field test of how each camera actually performs, plus a method you can use to test any phone before you buy.

...

All three phones sit under the $600 mark and target people who want a good camera without paying flagship money. They take completely different approaches to hardware, and that difference shows up in the photos.

- Google Pixel 9a ($499): 48MP f/1.7 main with OIS, 13MP ultrawide, no telephoto. Google leans on computational photography, the same software philosophy used on its $1,000 flagships. It adds macro and astrophotography modes you will not find on the other two.
- Apple iPhone 16e ($599): a single 48MP f/1.6 main camera with OIS and a 2x in-sensor crop. One lens, no ultrawide, no macro. Apple bets the single sensor plus processing is enough.
- Samsung Galaxy A56 ($499): 50MP f/1.8 main with OIS, 12MP ultrawide, and a 5MP macro. Three lenses on paper, though the macro is low resolution.

The pricing matters. The iPhone 16e costs $100 more than the other two yet ships with one camera, which is the core tension in this test.

...

Camera reviews get vague fast. “Great in low light” means nothing without a method. I used the same approach the professional reviewers did: shoot the identical scene with each phone handheld, then inspect the files side by side on a calibrated monitor. ... You see the actual pixels, not what you remember.

For this article I pulled the data from over 200 paired shots across daytime, sunset, low light, macro, portrait, and zoom scenarios published by Tom’s Guide, PhoneArena, and Amateur Photographer. The pattern held across all three sources, which is why the conclusions below are reliable rather than one reviewer’s taste.

...

## Comparison Table

| Test | Pixel 9a | iPhone 16e | Galaxy A56 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main camera | 48MP f/1.7 | 48MP f/1.6 | 50MP f/1.8 |
| Lens count | 2 (main, ultrawide) | 1 (main only) | 3 (main, ultra, macro) |
| Low light | Best | Good, color tints | Good |
| Portrait | Best | Weak (one lens) | Flexible |
| Zoom 8x+ | Hazy | Sharpest | Reaches 10x, soft |
| Macro | Strong (ultrawide) | None | Weak 5MP |
| Video | 4K 60fps | 4K 60fps | 4K 30fps |
| Price | $499 | $599 | $499 |

...

Pick the Pixel 9a if photography is your priority. It wins low light, macro, and portraits, and it costs $100 less than the iPhone. The trade-offs are slower 23W charging and a smaller 128GB base storage.

Pick the iPhone 16e only if you are locked into Apple and mostly shoot with the main camera. Its single lens is genuinely good in daylight and at moderate zoom, but you give up an ultrawide, macro, and better portraiture.

Pick the Galaxy A56 if you want the most complete package for the money: three lenses, a bright 120Hz screen, fast 45W charging, and bolder colors. It does not win any single camera category outright, but it never leaves you without the right tool.

## 1. Samsung Galaxy S25 FE — Best Overall When Under $600

Samsung Galaxy S25 FE

The Samsung Galaxy S25 FE is the safest all-around choice in this group when you can find the unlocked version at or below the $600 mark.

That distinction matters. The S25 FE gives U.S. buyers something many mid-range phones cannot: a more complete flagship-style experience backed by Samsung's enormous U.S. support ecosystem. It has a polished AMOLED display, strong day-to-day performance, capable cameras, IP-rated durability, wireless charging, and One UI's mature software experience.

It is not the phone with the biggest battery or the highest charging wattage here. Instead, Samsung gets the important everyday details right.

The display is excellent for streaming, social media, reading, and gaming, while the software feels much more mature than what you get from many aggressive value-focused brands. Samsung's Knox security, carrier availability, repair network, and long-term software commitment also make the S25 FE easier to recommend to someone who plans to keep a phone for several years.

The biggest problem is price. The unlocked 128GB version can sit above the $600 threshold at U.S. retailers, so this becomes the overall winner specifically when a promotion or retailer discount brings it into the target budget.

Why it stands out: It offers the most complete combination of display quality, cameras, software, durability, features, and U.S. support in this group.

Where it falls short: It does not have the enormous battery or ultra-fast charging of some of the international phones below, and its unlocked U.S. price can exceed $600.

Best for: buyers who want a dependable all-round Android phone and plan to keep it for several years.

Motorola Edge 70 Pro+ 5G

Its biggest attraction is the camera hardware. A triple-camera setup with a dedicated telephoto camera gives you more flexibility than the typical two-camera mid-range phone. A proper telephoto lens is especially useful for portraits, distant subjects, travel photography, and situations where digital zoom starts falling apart.

Motorola also puts considerable attention into the display and physical design. The high-refresh-rate panel feels fluid while scrolling and gaming, and the slim body makes the phone easier to handle than some of the enormous battery-focused devices in this price class.

The catch for U.S. shoppers is important: this particular Pro+ model should not be treated as equivalent to Motorola's officially sold U.S. Edge models. Import availability, carrier compatibility, warranty support, and regional software can vary.

## A Price-Busting Camera

Stefan Vazharov

A triple-lens camera stack is rare on a phone this cheap.

The camera stack on the 2026 Edge features a trio of high-resolution lenses—a 50-megapixel (MP) primary camera, a 50MP with an ultrawide lens, and a 10MP telephoto lens. (Plus, a 50MP selfie snapper in front.) That’s standard for most high-end phones, but many budget phones drop the telephoto lens to keep prices down, so that automatically puts the snappers in rarefied air. The Google Pixel 10a has only two rear cameras, and the iPhone 17e skates by with a single lens.

That doesn’t necessarily mean that the Edge’s camera is comparable to a flagship like the Samsung S26 Ultra or the Google Pixel 10 Pro, but the results are very solid for the money. Avid shutterbugs will miss the additional performance and post-processing you get from those cameras, but a casual photographer probably won’t see the difference in most cases. Again, this is a compromise, but it’s more than fair given that the Edge costs hundreds of dollars less than an elite phone.

...

My biggest gripe with the latest Moto Edge is its shortage of storage space. With a paltry 128GB hard drive, it lags far behind every other budget phone in this one specific sense, including the iPhone 17e, the Nothing Phone (4a), and the Pixel 10a.

...

The Moto Edge is a really nice option for budget-conscious upgraders who want a smaller form factor and a lower price, but don’t want to sacrifice versatility, especially in the camera department. The phone looks slick and has a durable build, so it’s a great choice for folks who prefer not to hide their phone in a case. And while I have reservations about its storage and Motorola’s long-term support plan, these are relatively minor issues when we’re talking about a $600 phone. If you aren’t a phone nerd digging into deep specs, you may not even notice the difference between this and a top Android that costs twice as much.
